title: Caesar Cipher Encryption
statement: Julius Caesar encrypted messages by shifting every letter a fixed number of positions down the alphabet, wrapping around from the end. Given a message and a shift value k, encrypt the message: every letter moves k positions forward (z wraps around to a), letter CASE is preserved, and every non-letter character (digits, spaces, punctuation) stays exactly as it is.
inputFormat:
Line 1: the message string s (letters, digits, spaces, punctuation).
Line 2: integer k (0-25).
outputFormat: One line: the encrypted string.
starter:
s = input().strip()
k = int(input().strip())
# TODO: encrypt and print the result
approach: Normalize each letter into 0-25, add k modulo 26, convert back. Non-letters pass through untouched.
steps: Read the string s and the shift k.
Create an empty result string.
Loop over every character ch in s.
Lowercase letter: its position is ord(ch) - ord('a'). Add k, take modulo 26 (this makes z wrap to a), then convert back with chr(... + ord('a')).
Uppercase letter: same trick with ord('A') so the case is preserved.
Any other character (space, digit, punctuation): append it unchanged.
Print the result on one line.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space — one pass over the string.
insight: The (ord - base + k) % 26 + base pattern is the whole trick — it reappears in many Accenture string-encoding questions.

title: Find the Second Largest
years: Classic repeat (2019-2024); base of the AXIS 'second largest' variants
statement: Given an array of integers, find the SECOND LARGEST distinct value. Duplicates of the largest do not count — the second largest must be strictly smaller than the largest. If every element is equal (no second largest exists), print -1.
inputFormat:
Line 1: integer n (array size).
Line 2: n space-separated integers.
outputFormat: One integer: the second largest distinct value, or -1.
starter:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: print the second largest distinct value (or -1)
solution:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
largest = None
second = None
for x in arr:
    if largest is None or x > largest:
        second = largest
        largest = x
    elif x != largest and (second is None or x > second):
        second = x
print(second if second is not None else -1)
approach: Track two champions in one pass: the largest so far and the best runner-up.
steps: Read n and the array.
Set largest = -1 and second = -1.
For each number x: if x beats largest, the old largest is demoted to second, and x becomes the new largest.
Otherwise, if x beats second AND x is not equal to largest (duplicates of the champion never count), promote x to second.
After the loop, print second — it stays -1 when no distinct second value exists.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space — one pass, two variables.
insight: The two-variable 'largest & runner-up' scan is the most repeated array pattern in Accenture papers. Sorting also works but costs O(n log n).

title: Move Hyphens to Front
years: Published PYQ (2022-2024 drives; official C/Java solutions on PrepInsta)
statement: Given a string containing lowercase letters and hyphens '-', move EVERY hyphen to the FRONT of the string while keeping the relative order of all other characters unchanged. Example: 'move-hyphens-to-front' becomes '---movehyphenstofront'.
inputFormat: One line: the string s.
outputFormat: One line: the transformed string.
starter:
s = input().strip()
# TODO: move every '-' to the front, keep other characters in order
solution:
s = input().strip()
hyphens = s.count('-')
letters = s.replace('-', '')
print('-' * hyphens + letters)
approach: Count the hyphens, strip them out, then print that many hyphens followed by the cleaned string.
steps: Read the string.
Count the hyphens: hyphens = s.count('-').
Build the letters-only string: s.replace('-', '').
Print '-' * hyphens followed by the letters string — Python repeats a string with *.
insight: The official published solutions erase characters one by one; count-and-rebuild is simpler and shows the 'partition by character class' pattern.

title: Autobiographical Number Check
statement: A number is AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL when the digit at position i tells how many times digit i appears in the number. Example 1210: it has one 0, two 1s, one 2 and zero 3s — the digits describe the number itself. Given a digit string, print the count of DISTINCT digits it contains if it is autobiographical, otherwise print 0. (A quick necessary condition: the digit-sum must equal the length.)
inputFormat: One line: the number as a digit string n.
outputFormat: One integer: count of distinct digits if autobiographical, else 0.
starter:
n = input().strip()
# TODO: print count of distinct digits if autobiographical, else 0
solution:
n = input().strip()
valid = len(n) == sum(int(d) for d in n) and all(
    n.count(str(i)) == int(n[i]) for i in range(len(n)))
if valid:
    print(len(set(n)))
else:
    print(0)
approach: Two checks: digit-sum equals length (quick reject), then every digit's claimed count matches its actual count. If both pass, count distinct digits.
steps: Read the number as a STRING (we need per-position digits).
Quick reject: sum of digits must equal the length — otherwise print 0.
For every position i from 0 to len-1: the digit at position i CLAIMS that digit i appears that many times.
Verify each claim by counting str(i) inside the string; any failed claim means print 0.
All claims passed: print how many DISTINCT digits the string contains (len(set(n))).
Note: some published variants only check sum==length; the true definition also verifies the counts (2200 passes the sum check but is NOT autobiographical).
complexity: O(L^2) worst case with L ≤ 10 — trivially fast.
insight: The published PrepInsta solution checks only sum==length; we implement the correct full definition — know the difference.

title: Rat Count House
statement: r rats must collect food from houses arranged in a row. Each rat eats exactly `unit` units of food, so together they need r × unit units. Walking from the FIRST house onward, they collect all the food of each house they visit. Print how many HOUSES they must visit to gather at least the required food. If the total food in all houses is still not enough, print 0.
inputFormat:
Line 1: r (number of rats).
Line 2: unit (units each rat eats).
Line 3: n (number of houses).
Line 4: n space-separated integers — food in each house in order.
outputFormat: One integer: houses visited to reach the requirement, or 0 if impossible.
starter:
r = int(input())
unit = int(input())
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: print houses needed to collect r*unit food (or 0 if impossible)
solution:
r = int(input())
unit = int(input())
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
if n == 0:
    print(-1)
else:
    needed = r * unit
    total = 0
    count = 0
    for food in arr:
        total += food
        count += 1
        if total >= needed:
            print(count)
            break
    else:
        print(0)
approach: Compute the target r*unit, then walk the array keeping a running sum; the first index where the sum reaches the target is the answer.
steps: Read r, unit, n and the array.
needed = r * unit — the total food requirement.
Walk the houses keeping total = food collected so far and count = houses visited.
The moment total >= needed, print count and stop — no need to visit further houses.
If the loop finishes without reaching the target, food is insufficient: print 0.
insight: A 'running sum until threshold' scan — the same skeleton solves fuel-station and minimum-houses style questions.

title: Password Validator
statement:
Validate a password against ALL of these rules:
1. At least 4 characters long.
2. At least one digit (0-9).
3. At least one CAPITAL letter.
4. No space and no slash '/'.
5. The FIRST character must not be a digit.
Print 1 if every rule passes, otherwise 0.
inputFormat: One line: the password string s.
outputFormat: 1 (valid) or 0 (invalid).
starter:
s = input().strip()
# TODO: print 1 if the password satisfies all 5 rules, else 0
approach: Check the two positional rules first (length, first char), then the forbidden characters, then confirm the required character classes exist.
steps: Read the password.
Rule 1: length must be at least 4 — otherwise print 0.
Rule 5: if the FIRST character is a digit, print 0.
Rule 4: if the string contains a space or a slash '/', print 0.
Rules 2+3: scan the string — at least one digit AND at least one uppercase letter must exist.
Everything passed: print 1; any failure: print 0.
insight: Multi-rule validators are pure translation practice: each English rule becomes one boolean check. Order the cheap positional rules first.

title: Sum of Numbers Divisible By N
statement: Given two integers m and n, calculate the sum of ALL numbers from 1 to m (inclusive) that are divisible by n. Example: m=20, n=5 -> 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 = 50.
inputFormat:
Line 1: integer m (upper bound).
Line 2: integer n (divisor).
outputFormat: One integer: the sum.
starter:
m = int(input())
n = int(input())
# TODO: print the sum of 1..m divisible by n
solution:
m = int(input())
n = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(n, m + 1, n):
    total += i
print(total)
approach: Walk the multiples of n directly — range(n, m+1, n) — and sum them.
steps: Read m and n.
Start a total at 0.
Instead of testing every number, step through the MULTIPLES of n directly: range(n, m+1, n) gives n, 2n, 3n... up to m.
Add each multiple to the total.
Print the total.
Equivalent beginner version: loop i from 1 to m and add i only when i % n == 0.
complexity: O(m/n) time with the multiples loop, O(1) space.
insight: The % filter loop is the most beginner pattern in the pool; the multiples-range upgrade shows you can optimise.

title: Palindrome Check
statement: A string is a PALINDROME when it reads the same forwards and backwards ('level', 'abba'). Given a string, print 1 if it is a palindrome, otherwise 0.
inputFormat: One line: the string s (lowercase letters).
outputFormat: 1 if palindrome, else 0.
starter:
s = input().strip()
# TODO: print 1 if palindrome else 0
solution:
s = input().strip()
print(1 if s == s[::-1] else 0)
approach: Compare the string with its reverse — or walk two pointers from both ends toward the middle.
steps: Read the string.
Reverse it with slicing: s[::-1].
If s equals its reverse, print 1; else print 0.
Alternative: two pointers i=0 and j=len-1 — move inward while characters match; any mismatch means 0.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the slice (O(1) with two pointers).
insight: s[::-1] reversal appears in half of all Accenture string questions — learn it once, reuse everywhere.

title: Anagram Check
statement: Two strings are ANAGRAMS when one is a rearrangement of the other — same letters, same counts, different order ('listen' / 'silent'). Given two strings, print Yes if they are anagrams, otherwise No.
inputFormat:
Line 1: first string.
Line 2: second string.
outputFormat: Yes or No.
starter:
a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
# TODO: print Yes if anagrams else No
solution:
a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
print('Yes' if sorted(a) == sorted(b) else 'No')
approach: Anagrams contain identical letter counts — sorting both strings makes the comparison trivial.
steps: Read both strings.
sorted(a) turns each string into a sorted list of characters — anagrams sort identically.
Compare the two sorted lists; equal means anagram.
Print Yes or No accordingly.
Alternative: count letters with a dictionary (or collections.Counter) and compare the counts.
complexity: O(n log n) with sorting, O(n) with counting.
insight: sorted() comparison is the 2-line interview answer; Counter is the scalable one — know both.

title: Count Vowels & Consonants
statement: Given a sentence, count the VOWELS (a, e, i, o, u — any case) and the CONSONANTS (every other alphabet letter). Digits, spaces and punctuation are ignored. Print the two counts separated by a space.
inputFormat: One line: the sentence s.
outputFormat: One line: vowel-count space consonant-count.
starter:
s = input().strip()
# TODO: print vowel count and consonant count separated by a space
approach: One pass, two counters — classify each alphabetic character, ignore everything else.
steps: Read the sentence.
Start counters v = 0 and c = 0.
For each character: if it is NOT alphabetic (ch.isalpha() false), skip it.
If the lowercase form is in 'aeiou', increment v; otherwise increment c.
Print v and c separated by a space.
insight: Character-classification loops (isalpha/isdigit/isupper) power a third of the string pool.

title: Kth Largest Number
statement: Given an array and an integer k, return the k-th GREATEST element counting DISTINCT values: k = 0 means the greatest, k = 1 the second greatest, and so on. If k is out of range, print -1. Example: array 74 85 102 99 101 56 84 with k = 2 returns 99 — only 102 and 101 are greater.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: n space-separated integers.
Line 3: k.
outputFormat: The k-th greatest distinct value, or -1.
starter:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
k = int(input())
# TODO: print the k-th greatest distinct value or -1
solution:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
k = int(input())
unique = sorted(set(arr), reverse=True)
if 0 <= k < len(unique):
    print(unique[k])
else:
    print(-1)
approach: Deduplicate, sort descending, index k — with a bounds check for -1.
steps: Read n, the array and k.
set(arr) removes duplicates — 'distinct values' is the key requirement.
sorted(..., reverse=True) orders them greatest-first.
If k is a valid index (0 <= k < length), print unique[k]; otherwise print -1.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
insight: Deduplicate-then-sort is the standard answer; a heap gives O(n log k) but is never required at this difficulty.

title: Count Bubble Sort Swaps
statement: Simulate BUBBLE SORT on an array of distinct integers (ascending) and count how many SWAPS happen in total. Bubble sort repeatedly walks the array, swapping neighbours that are out of order, pushing the largest remaining value to the end each pass.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: n distinct space-separated integers.
outputFormat: One integer: total number of swaps performed.
starter:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: bubble-sort the array, print total swaps
approach: Implement bubble sort literally and add 1 to a counter on every swap — simulation, not cleverness.
steps: Read n and the array.
Outer loop i from 0 to n-2: one pass per largest element.
Inner loop j from 0 to n-2-i: compare neighbours arr[j] and arr[j+1].
If arr[j] > arr[j+1], swap them (Python tuple swap) and add 1 to swaps.
After all passes, print swaps.
Fact worth knowing: the swap count equals the number of INVERSION pairs in the array.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) space — fine for n ≤ 1000.
insight: Simulation questions reward literal translation of the described algorithm — no optimisation asked, none needed.

title: Find the Key (Digit Position Sums)
statement: The KEY of a number is the absolute difference between the sum of its digits at ODD positions and the sum of its digits at EVEN positions — positions counted from the RIGHT, starting at 1 (the last digit is position 1). Example: 5473 -> from the right: 3 is position 1 (odd), 7 is position 2 (even), 4 is position 3 (odd), 5 is position 4 (even). Odd sum = 3 + 4 = 7, even sum = 7 + 5 = 12, key = |7 - 12| = 5.
inputFormat: One line: the number n (read it as a string — it can be very long).
outputFormat: One integer: the key.
starter:
num = input().strip()
# TODO: print |sum of odd-position digits - sum of even-position digits|, positions from the right
approach: Walk digits from the right, alternating odd/even buckets, then print the absolute difference.
steps: Read the number as a STRING.
Reverse it so index 0 is the LAST digit (position 1 = odd).
Walk with enumerate: position = index + 1.
Odd position digits add to odd_sum; even position digits add to even_sum.
Print abs(odd_sum - even_sum).
complexity: O(d) time, O(1) space (d = digit count).
insight: The 'find the key' family (digit sums, position sums, digit differences) all reuse this walk-the-digits skeleton.

title: Exponent of 2 in a Number
statement: For a given number N, find the largest exponent e such that 2^e divides N exactly. Example: 12 = 4 × 3 = 2^2 × 3, so the answer is 2. An odd number has exponent 0.
inputFormat: One line: integer N.
outputFormat: One integer: the exponent e.
starter:
n = int(input())
# TODO: print the largest e with 2^e dividing n
solution:
n = int(input())
count = 0
while n > 0 and n % 2 == 0:
    n //= 2
    count += 1
print(count)
approach: Keep dividing by 2 while it divides evenly — the division count is the answer.
steps: Read N.
Start count = 0.
While N is even (N % 2 == 0): divide N by 2 and add 1 to count.
When N turns odd, no factor of 2 remains — print count.
Odd inputs never enter the loop and correctly print 0.
insight: The divide-while-divisible loop generalises to 'exponent of any prime p' — change 2 to p.

title: Sum Until Single Digit
statement: Repeatedly replace the number by the SUM of its digits until only a single digit remains. Example: 9875 -> 9+8+7+5 = 29 -> 2+9 = 11 -> 1+1 = 2. Print the final single digit.
inputFormat: One line: integer N.
outputFormat: One digit: the final single-digit result.
starter:
n = int(input())
# TODO: reduce to a single digit by repeated digit sums
solution:
n = int(input())
while n >= 10:
    n = sum(int(d) for d in str(n))
print(n)
approach: While the number has 2+ digits, replace it with its digit sum.
steps: Read N.
While n >= 10: convert to string, sum its digits, store back into n.
The loop ends when n is a single digit — print it.
Each pass shrinks huge numbers dramatically, so the loop runs only a handful of times.
Bonus fact: for n > 0 the answer equals 1 + (n - 1) % 9 — the digital-root formula.
complexity: Effectively O(1) — at most ~4 iterations for any input.
insight: Digit-sum iteration (and its O(1) digital-root formula) is a favourite trick question.

title: Trim From Both Ends
statement: Given a string and two counts n1 and n2, remove exactly n1 characters from the LEFT end and n2 characters from the RIGHT end, then print what remains. Example: 'helloWorld' with n1=3, n2=2 becomes 'loWor'.
inputFormat:
Line 1: the string s.
Line 2: n1 and n2 separated by a space.
outputFormat: One line: the trimmed string.
starter:
s = input().strip()
n1, n2 = map(int, input().split())
# TODO: remove n1 chars from the left and n2 from the right, print the rest
solution:
s = input().strip()
n1, n2 = map(int, input().split())
print(s[n1:len(s) - n2])
approach: One slice does everything: s[n1 : len(s)-n2].
steps: Read the string and the two counts (they arrive on one line — split them).
The kept region starts at index n1.
It ends just before len(s) - n2.
Print s[n1 : len(s) - n2] — Python slicing handles both ends at once.
Sanity check with the sample: 'helloWorld'[3:8] = 'loWor'.
insight: Slicing (s[a:b], s[::-1], s[a:b:c]) is the highest-leverage Python skill for this pool.

title: Binary to Decimal
statement: Convert a binary number (given as a string of 0s and 1s) to its decimal value. Example: 1010 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 10.
inputFormat: One line: the binary string b.
outputFormat: One integer: the decimal value.
starter:
b = input().strip()
# TODO: print the decimal value of the binary string
solution:
b = input().strip()
value = 0
for bit in b:
    value = value * 2 + int(bit)
print(value)
approach: Walk left to right doubling the accumulator and adding each bit (Horner's method) — int(b, 2) is the one-line alternative.
steps: Read the binary string.
Start value = 0.
For each bit from LEFT to RIGHT: value = value * 2 + int(bit) — doubling shifts everything one place, the new bit fills the gap.
Manual check with 1010: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 5 -> 10 — matches.
One-liner alternative: print(int(b, 2)) — the 2 says the input is base 2.
insight: int(s, base) also converts hex (16) and octal (8) — one tool, many exam questions.

title: Leaders in an Array
years: AXIS 2024 real question family (leader element; LeetCode interview report Nov 2024)
statement: An element is a LEADER if it is strictly greater than EVERY element to its right. The last element is always a leader (nothing is to its right). Given an array, print all leaders in their ORIGINAL left-to-right order. Example: 16 17 4 3 5 2 -> leaders are 17 (everything after it is smaller), 5 (only 2 after it) and 2.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: n space-separated integers.
outputFormat: One line: the leaders, space-separated, in original order.
starter:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: print all leaders (greater than everything to their right) in original order
solution:
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
leaders = []
best = float('-inf')
for x in reversed(arr):
    if x > best:
        leaders.append(x)
        best = x
leaders.reverse()
print(*leaders)
approach: Scan from the RIGHT keeping the best-so-far; any element beating the best is a leader. Reverse the collected list at the end.
steps: Read n and the array.
Walk from the LAST element to the first (reversed).
Track best = the largest value seen so far on the right side.
If the current element is strictly greater than best, it is a leader — append it and update best.
The collected list is right-to-left, so reverse it before printing.
print(*leaders) prints them space-separated.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space — the right-to-left scan avoids the O(n^2) double loop.
insight: This exact family appeared in the AXIS 2024 coding slot ('largest element such that every element to its right is smaller'). The reverse-scan is the pattern to internalise.

title: Armstrong Number
statement: An ARMSTRONG number equals the sum of its own digits each raised to the power of the digit count. Example: 153 -> 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153. Given a number, print Yes if it is an Armstrong number, otherwise No.
inputFormat: One line: integer N.
outputFormat: Yes or No.
starter:
n = input().strip()
# TODO: print Yes if N is an Armstrong number else No
approach: Power p = number of digits; compare N with the sum of each digit raised to p.
steps: Read N as a string to count digits easily.
p = len(n) — the digit count.
Sum each digit raised to the p-th power: sum(int(d) ** p for d in n).
If that sum equals int(n), print Yes; else print No.
Single-digit numbers (0-9) are trivially Armstrong — d^1 = d.
complexity: O(d) time where d = digit count.
insight: The 'digits raised to digit-count' pattern also appears in narcissistic-number and disarium-number variants.

title: Print Fibonacci Series
statement: Print the first n terms of the FIBONACCI series, where each term is the sum of the previous two, starting from 0 and 1. Example: n = 7 prints 0 1 1 2 3 5 8.
inputFormat: One line: integer n.
outputFormat: One line: the first n Fibonacci terms separated by spaces.
starter:
n = int(input())
# TODO: print the first n Fibonacci terms space-separated
solution:
n = int(input())
a, b = 0, 1
out = []
for _ in range(n):
    out.append(str(a))
    a, b = b, a + b
print(' '.join(out))
approach: Keep two rolling variables (a, b); print a, then shift the pair forward n times.
steps: Read n.
Set a = 0, b = 1 — the first two terms.
Repeat n times: record a, then move the window with a, b = b, a + b.
Join the recorded terms with spaces and print.
The tuple assignment updates BOTH variables at once — no temp variable needed.
insight: The two-variable roll is the skeleton of many series questions (Tribonacci, special sums) in the pool.

title: Prime Check
statement: A PRIME number is greater than 1 and divisible only by 1 and itself. Given N, print Prime or Not Prime.
inputFormat: One line: integer N.
outputFormat: Prime or Not Prime.
starter:
n = int(input())
# TODO: print Prime or Not Prime
approach: Trial division up to sqrt(n): if any d from 2 to sqrt(n) divides n, it is composite.
steps: Read N. Numbers below 2 are NOT prime — handle 0 and 1 first.
Try every divisor d starting at 2 while d*d <= n (d up to the square root).
If any d divides N evenly, print Not Prime and stop.
No divisor found by sqrt -> Prime.
The d*d <= n bound is the efficiency trick: divisors come in pairs, one of each pair is always <= sqrt(n).
insight: The d*d <= n loop avoids floating-point sqrt entirely — the clean way to write trial division.

title: Reverse the Word Order
statement: Given a sentence, reverse the ORDER of its words (each word itself stays intact). Example: 'Hello World' becomes 'World Hello'.
inputFormat: One line: the sentence (words separated by single spaces).
outputFormat: One line: words in reversed order, single-spaced.
starter:
sentence = input().strip()
# TODO: print the words in reversed order
solution:
words = input().strip().split()
print(' '.join(reversed(words)))
approach: Split into a list of words, reverse the list, join with spaces — the split-transform-join trio.
steps: Read the sentence.
words = sentence.split() — splits on whitespace into a list.
Reverse with reversed(words) or words[::-1].
' '.join(...) glues them back with single spaces.
Print the result.
insight: Split-transform-join is the highest-frequency string pipeline in Python interview answers.

title: Run-Length String Compression
statement: Compress a string by replacing each RUN of repeated characters with the character followed by its count. Example: 'aaabb' becomes 'a3b2'; 'abcd' becomes 'a1b1c1d1' (count 1 is still written).
inputFormat: One line: the string s.
outputFormat: One line: the compressed string.
starter:
s = input().strip()
# TODO: print the run-length compressed string
solution:
s = input().strip()
out = []
count = 1
for i in range(1, len(s)):
    if s[i] == s[i - 1]:
        count += 1
    else:
        out.append(s[i - 1] + str(count))
        count = 1
out.append(s[-1] + str(count))
print(''.join(out))
approach: Walk the string counting runs of identical characters; when the character changes, flush 'char+count'.
steps: Read the string.
Start count = 1 for the first character.
From index 1 onward: if s[i] equals the previous character, increment count.
Otherwise the run ended — append the previous character and its count, reset count to 1.
After the loop, flush the final run (it never triggers the 'change' branch).
Join and print.
insight: Run-length encoding is the classic 'flush on change' pattern — the same skeleton solves grouped-output and streak-counting questions.

title: Find the Missing Number
statement: The numbers 1..n are all present except ONE, which is missing. Given n and the remaining numbers (in any order), print the missing number.
inputFormat:
Line 1: n.
Line 2: n-1 distinct space-separated integers from 1..n.
outputFormat: One integer: the missing number.
starter:
n = int(input())
nums = list(map(int, input().split()))
# TODO: print the missing number
solution:
n = int(input())

approach: Dynamic programming with two variables: at each house take max of skipping it or robbing it plus best up to i-2.
steps: Read n and the house values.
Keep prev1 = best up to previous house, prev2 = best up to house before that.
For each house value x compute cur = max(prev1, prev2 + x).
Shift prev2 to prev1 and prev1 to cur.
Repeat for all houses.
Print prev1 as the answer.
Only two variables needed instead of a full table.
insight: Each house is skip-or-take - only the last two answers matter.
